{
  "title": "When Does Consistency Checking Help? A Diagnostic Study of Detection Coverage for Temporal Chain-of-Thought Extraction Errors",
  "core_problem": "Multiple verification paradigms — consistency-based (path-consistency, ILP, SMT), probabilistic (credal intervals + EDL), and neural (abductive reflection) — have been proposed for catching temporal extraction errors in neuro-symbolic QA, but a fundamental empirical question remains unanswered: what fraction of extraction errors actually produce detectable inconsistencies, and under what conditions? Eirew et al. (EMNLP 2025) provide an important empirical observation — global consistency enforcement via ILP improves results on exhaustively-annotated datasets (NT-6: +4.7 F1; OmniTemp: +4.6) but global-pipeline approaches underperform pairwise CoT on sparsely-annotated data (MATRES: 66.4 vs. 70.3) — but they offer no formal explanation for WHY this density-dependent pattern exists. Crucially, Nebel & Bürckert (JACM 1995) prove that for basic Allen relations (a subset of ORD-Horn), path-consistency is COMPLETE for detecting all inconsistencies in O(n³) time. This means SMT solvers like Z3 add ZERO additional detection power — the detection coverage limits are FUNDAMENTAL to the constraint language, not artifacts of any particular solver. The answer to 'when does consistency checking help?' therefore requires understanding three poorly-characterized factors: (1) composition tightness — what fraction of Allen composition table entries yield unique relations (enabling detection) vs. disjunctions masking errors; precisely, 97 of 169 basic-relation compositions (57.4%) are singletons (computed from Alspaugh's composition table), with remaining entries yielding result sets of size 3 (42 entries), 5 (24), 9 (3), or 13 (3); (2) the interaction between constraint graph density and detection probability — formally, P_detect ≈ 1-(1-d²·τ)^(N-2) where d is density, τ is average composition tightness (~0.88 under uniform relation distribution), and N is event count; and (3) how different error types (omission, misclassification, hallucination) interact differently with graph structure. Additionally, a prerequisite question — whether LLMs can reliably formalize temporal statements into Allen's vocabulary at all — remains open: LLM-as-formalizer underperforms LLM-as-solver in 15/24 CSP combinations (arXiv 2505.13252), though Allen's fixed 13-relation vocabulary may be more tractable than general CSPs.",
  "opportunity": "The extraction bottleneck for temporal QA is well-established (TMLR 2025; NeSTR, AAAI 2026), and several verification approaches exist (abductive reflection, probabilistic signals, consistency constraints). Converging evidence raises serious questions about consistency-based verification's value, but existing analyses remain purely empirical, leaving the field without a principled framework for deciding WHEN to invest in verification.

Eirew et al. (EMNLP 2025) provide the key empirical observation: their GlobalConsistency method (global graph generation + ILP with Allen transitivity constraints) achieves 64.1 F1 on exhaustively-annotated NT-6 vs. 57.9 for pairwise CoT (+6.2), but only 66.4 vs. 70.3 on sparsely-annotated MATRES (-3.9). CRITICALLY, this comparison conflates two effects: (a) paradigm choice (global vs. pairwise extraction) and (b) consistency enforcement (ILP constraints). Within the global paradigm, ILP always helps (ZSL-Timeline 59.0 → GlobalConsistency 66.4 on MATRES, +7.4). The density-dependent pattern emerges from the paradigm comparison, not from consistency alone. Separately, Kougia et al. (BioNLP 2024) show a genuine case where ILP hurts PAIRWISE predictions: Llama CoT drops from 0.615 to 0.549 F1 on clinical temporal data.

What's MISSING from both studies — and what our work provides — is the formal framework that EXPLAINS these empirical patterns. Allen's composition table has a precise mathematical structure: of the 169 basic-relation compositions, exactly 97 (57.4%) yield singletons that guarantee error detection, while 42 yield size-3 sets, 24 yield size-5, 3 yield size-9, and 3 the full 13-relation set that masks all errors. By analyzing composition tightness as a function of relation type distribution and graph density, we derive a detection probability formula that predicts exactly when verification crosses the cost-benefit threshold. Neither Eirew et al. nor Kougia et al. provide this analysis. Importantly, Nebel & Bürckert (JACM 1995) prove that for basic Allen relations (which form a subset of the ORD-Horn class), path-consistency is COMPLETE — meaning our analysis characterizes the limits of ANY consistency-based approach, whether implemented via O(n³) path-consistency, ILP, or SMT. This solver-agnostic generality strengthens rather than weakens the contribution.

Further supporting evidence: (a) 'A Reality Check of LMs as Formalizers' (arXiv 2505.13252) shows LLM-as-formalizer underperforms LLM-as-solver in 15/24 CSP combinations, though Allen's interval algebra (fixed 13-relation vocabulary) was not specifically tested, and the follow-up (arXiv 2603.23844) shows formalizers scale in structured domains; (b) TIME 2025 shows LLMs achieve only 52-82% on interval temporal logic validity recognition with no sensitivity to complexity class; (c) GraFT (ICML 2025) achieves 99%+ accuracy on NL-to-temporal-logic with grammar-constrained decoding, suggesting constrained output formats can dramatically improve formalization; (d) ChronoSense (ACL 2025) shows GPT-4o achieves 0.877 accuracy on Allen relation classification WITH explicit intervals given (average of 13 Allen-specific zero-shot accuracies from v2 Table 2, ranging from 0.69 for Equals to 0.956 for After) — but extraction from natural language text is fundamentally harder (no existing study measures this gap).

Beyond temporal reasoning, the density-threshold framework generalizes to any constraint-based verification domain where composition tightness can be characterized: RCC-8 spatial relations (8×8 composition table with 27/64 singletons = 42.2%, yielding τ_uniform ≈ 0.71 vs. Allen's 57.4% and τ ≈ 0.88, predicting lower detection coverage for spatial verification at equivalent densities), event coreference transitivity (where ILP enforcement of transitive closure improves performance by up to 3.6% B³ / 16.5% cluster F-score — Finkel & Manning, 2008), or entity relation consistency checking. Our composition tightness analysis provides a template for principled cost-benefit assessment in each domain.",
  "landscape": "NeSTR (AAAI 2026) uses symbolic temporal predicates with neural abductive reflection, achieving 85.2 EM (GPT-4o-mini macro avg) and 84.5 EM / 88.8 F1 (Qwen3-14B macro avg) zero-shot on TempReason/TimeQA — no formal verification. TISER (ACL 2025) achieves 91.1 EM macro average but requires fine-tuning on GPT-4-generated data; zero-shot Qwen2.5-7B achieves only 52.3 EM. arXiv:2605.04243 (May 2026; UNREVIEWED single-author preprint from a non-research-institution affiliation, no code released) introduces a PIS framework with per-step dual-stream verification — reporting 100% on synthetic benchmarks but only 75.1% on TimeX-NLI and ~50% on TRACIE. AdapTime (ACL 2026 Findings) uses adaptive prompt-based temporal reasoning achieving 85.4 EM on TimeQA-Easy with DeepSeek-V3. TempCoT (SIGIR 2025) uses point algebra with semantic fact retrieval. 'Unreasonable effectiveness' (TMLR 2025) found Allen's interval algebra neuro-symbolic pipeline produced NO improvement over neural baselines — extraction is the bottleneck.

On temporal relation extraction specifically: Eirew et al. (EMNLP 2025) test five zero-shot paradigms with DeepSeek-R1 on MATRES: pairwise CoT (70.3 F1), ZSL-Global (61.0), ZSL-Timeline (59.0), SelfConsistency via majority vote (61.2), and GlobalConsistency via ILP (66.4). On exhaustively-annotated datasets, GlobalConsistency matches supervised methods: 64.1 on NT-6, 79.2 on OmniTemp. They attribute the sparse-vs-dense gap to 'annotation distance restriction' and event count sensitivity, but provide no formal framework for the density-dependent effect. Their ILP uses Allen transitivity constraints but without analyzing composition tightness or detection coverage by error type. MATRES has 79% missing relations; OmniTemp has 0% (exhaustive annotation). Kougia et al. (BioNLP 2024) show ILP hurts Llama pairwise predictions on clinical data (0.615 → 0.549 F1), a distinct phenomenon from Eirew et al.'s paradigm comparison.

On formalization: VeriCoT (arXiv 2025) reports 15-45% verification pass rates formalizing general CoT to FOL. Amonkar et al. (arXiv 2505.13252, v4 March 2026) show LLM-as-formalizer underperforms LLM-as-solver in 15/24 CSP combinations — but tested scheduling, trip planning, and logic puzzles, NOT Allen relation formalization. The follow-up (arXiv 2603.23844) shows formalizers scale dramatically in structured planning (100% at 100 blocks). GraFT (ICML 2025, PMLR vol. 267) achieves 99%+ accuracy on NL-to-temporal-logic via grammar-constrained decoding. TIME 2025 shows 52-82% accuracy on Halpern-Shoham interval temporal logic validity recognition. ChronoSense (ACL 2025, v2) shows GPT-4o achieves 0.877 accuracy classifying Allen relations with explicit intervals given (average of 13 Allen-specific zero-shot accuracies from v2 Table 2, ranging from 0.69 for Equals to 0.956 for After; the 0.86 figure from v1 is the all-task average including non-Allen tasks) — but no study measures performance on extraction from natural language text without given intervals.

On tractability and solver choice: Nebel & Bürckert (JACM 1995) prove that the 13 basic Allen relations form a subset of the ORD-Horn class, for which path-consistency is COMPLETE and runs in O(n³). This means that for networks of basic Allen relations, path-consistency determines satisfiability exactly — Z3 SMT, ILP, and other solvers provide identical detection power. Our detection coverage analysis therefore characterizes the fundamental limits of ANY consistency-based approach, not the properties of a specific solver.

VERGE (arXiv 2026) shows Z3+MCS correction converges monotonically in ~6 iterations. 'Empirical Characterization of Temporal Constraint Processing in LLMs' (arXiv 2511.10654) finds bimodal performance and extreme prompt brittleness.

Key gap: Eirew et al. observe density-dependent effects empirically; our contribution is the FORMAL FRAMEWORK (composition table tightness analysis, detection probability formula P_detect ≈ 1-(1-d²·τ)^(N-2)) that explains WHY — and this framework applies to any consistency-based approach, not just a specific solver. Additionally, no study tests formalization feasibility specifically for Allen relations from temporal QA text, and no study decomposes detection coverage by error type (omission vs. misclassification vs. hallucination). The framework further generalizes beyond temporal reasoning to any qualitative constraint calculus with a composition table (RCC-8, event coreference, etc.).",
  "inspired_by": "Convergence of empirical observations LACKING formal explanation: (1) Eirew et al. (EMNLP 2025) show density-dependent effects across MATRES/NT-6/OmniTemp but provide no formal framework — just the observation that 'models encoding global information are more sensitive to event count'; (2) Kougia et al. (BioNLP 2024) show ILP hurts pairwise predictions on clinical data (0.615→0.549) but don't explain why; (3) CSP formalization literature (arXiv 2505.13252) shows formalization can fail but didn't test Allen's interval algebra specifically; (4) TIME 2025 shows LLMs reason poorly about interval temporal logic; (5) Nebel & Bürckert (JACM 1995) prove path-consistency completeness for ORD-Horn, implying the detection limits are fundamental to the constraint language. The key realization: Allen's composition table has a known precise mathematical structure — 97/169 compositions (57.4%) are singletons, with remaining entries yielding exactly size-3, 5, 9, or 13 result sets — and this structure DIRECTLY determines detection probability as a function of graph density. The detection probability formula P_detect ≈ 1-(1-d²·τ)^(N-2) is solver-agnostic (holding for path-consistency, ILP, and SMT alike), making the analysis more general. This formal analysis fills the gap between 'we observe density matters' (Eirew et al.) and 'here's exactly why, and here's the threshold formula a practitioner can use.' Pattern: analogous to how 'Right for the Wrong Reasons' (McCoy et al., ACL 2019) provided diagnostic insight into NLI beyond mere accuracy numbers.",
  "approach": "We propose a diagnostic study — TemporalCoT-Verify — that answers 'When does consistency checking help catch temporal extraction errors in LLM chain-of-thought reasoning?' through four contributions: a formalization feasibility pilot, constraint graph density characterization, a formal detection coverage framework based on Allen's composition table tightness, and systematic empirical validation. The pipeline is a research vehicle for this analysis, not a SOTA-seeking system. Our detection coverage framework is SOLVER-AGNOSTIC: Nebel & Bürckert (JACM 1995) prove that for basic Allen relations (subset of ORD-Horn), path-consistency is COMPLETE for detecting all inconsistencies in O(n³). This means the detection coverage limits we characterize are FUNDAMENTAL to the constraint language — they hold identically for path-consistency, ILP (Eirew et al.), or SMT solvers. Practitioners can use the simplest adequate solver.

**Stage 0 (Formalization Feasibility Pilot — Prerequisite Validation):** We conduct a pilot measuring whether LLMs can reliably formalize temporal statements from QA text into Allen's 13-relation vocabulary. Amonkar et al. (arXiv 2505.13252) show formalization challenges on general CSPs, but Allen's fixed 13-way vocabulary is substantially more constrained. ChronoSense (ACL 2025, v2) shows GPT-4o achieves 0.877 accuracy classifying Allen relations WITH explicit intervals given (average of 13 Allen-specific zero-shot accuracies from Table 2, ranging from 0.69 for Equals to 0.956 for After); we estimate extraction from natural language text (without explicit intervals) will yield 0.55-0.70 accuracy with structured-output constraints and 0.40-0.60 unconstrained, based on: (a) the gap between structured classification and open-ended extraction observed across NLU tasks; (b) the additional difficulty of identifying implicit temporal boundaries; (c) VeriCoT's 15-45% pass rate on the harder task of general CoT→FOL formalization (Allen classification is substantially easier). We test on 100 temporal statements sampled from TGQA/TempReason/TimeQA with three decoding strategies: (a) unconstrained LLM output (GPT-4o-mini, Qwen3-14B); (b) structured-output JSON schema constraints (13 relations as enum); (c) grammar-constrained decoding (GraFT-style, motivated by GraFT's 99%+ on NL→LTL at ICML 2025). We also catalog failure modes specific to temporal formalization: implicit relations, vague temporal references ('around that time'), relative expressions ('shortly after'), and missing event instantiation. If formalization success is <60% even with constrained decoding, this is itself a key finding that quantifies the formalization gap for Allen's relations specifically.

**Stage 1 (Constraint Graph Density Characterization):** We measure the density of temporal constraint graphs extractable from standard QA benchmarks (TGQA, TempReason L2/L3, TimeQA Easy/Hard), reporting: (a) average number of temporal entities per question; (b) average extractable Allen relations; (c) graph density ratio (edges / max possible edges); (d) constraint redundancy via transitivity. We connect our measurements to Eirew et al.'s finding that MATRES has 79% missing relations vs. OmniTemp's 0%, showing that temporal QA benchmarks likely have density profiles closer to MATRES than OmniTemp — which has direct implications for verification utility via our detection probability formula.

**Stage 2 (Detection Coverage Framework — Primary Novel Contribution):** We provide the first formal analysis of consistency-based detection coverage for temporal extraction errors, grounded in the mathematical structure of Allen's composition table. This analysis applies to ANY consistency-based approach — path-consistency, ILP, or SMT — since Nebel & Bürckert (JACM 1995) prove that path-consistency alone is complete for basic Allen relations.

(a) **Composition tightness analysis**: Allen's 169 basic-relation compositions yield result sets of exactly 1, 3, 5, 9, or 13 relations (a known mathematical property). We compute these PRECISELY from the published composition table (Alspaugh's Table 4b): 97 entries (57.4%) are singletons — broken down by relation as p(22), P(22), d(9), D(9), m(6), M(6), o(5), O(5), s(3), S(3), f(3), F(3), e(1) — with 42 entries (24.9%) yielding size-3 sets, 24 (14.2%) yielding size-5, 3 (1.8%) yielding size-9 (the 'concur' set), and 3 (1.8%) yielding the full 13-relation set. Singletons guarantee detection of any wrong relation; the full set provides zero detection capability. The per-triangle detection probability for a uniformly random misclassification is (13-|S|)/12, giving: size-1 → 1.0, size-3 → 0.833, size-5 → 0.667, size-9 → 0.333, size-13 → 0. The unweighted average composition tightness is τ_uniform = [97×1.0 + 42×0.833 + 24×0.667 + 3×0.333 + 3×0]/169 = 149/169 ≈ 0.88. For empirical analysis, we compute a weighted τ_w using the observed relation frequency distribution from each benchmark, since real data is skewed toward before/after.

(b) **Detection probability formula**: For N events, graph density d, and average composition tightness τ, the probability of detecting a wrong relation R(A,C) via at least one triangle A-B-C is: P_detect ≈ 1 - (1 - d²·τ)^(N-2). This formula explains the Eirew et al. results quantitatively: for sparse MATRES-like graphs (N≈22, d≈0.21 given 79% missing), P_detect ≈ 0.55; for dense OmniTemp-like graphs (N≈16, d≈1.0), P_detect approaches 1.0.

(c) **Prospective predictions for temporal QA benchmarks**: We pre-commit to specific P_detect predictions for each benchmark BEFORE running experiments, based on preliminary N and d estimates from dataset documentation and sampling:

| Benchmark       | Est. N | Est. d | Predicted P_detect | Prediction |
|-----------------|--------|--------|--------------------|------------|
| TGQA            | 8      | 0.35   | 0.50               | Moderate detection; verification may provide modest uplift |
| TempReason L2   | 5      | 0.33   | 0.26               | Near threshold; marginal benefit expected |
| TempReason L3   | 5      | 0.30   | 0.22               | Below threshold; verification likely not cost-effective |
| TimeQA Easy     | 5      | 0.25   | 0.16               | Well below threshold; verification not justified |
| TimeQA Hard     | 6      | 0.30   | 0.28               | Near threshold; may show small uplift |

Estimation basis: TGQA stories are generated from YAGO11k subgraphs with 5-28 temporal events per story (TG-LLM, ACL 2024) and ~9 temporal facts per sample; N≈8 reflects the median entity count, d≈0.35 reflects extractable pairwise relations relative to maximum edges. TempReason subjects have ~5.3 temporal facts (Tan et al., 2023); L2 (time-event) has slightly higher extractable density than L3 (event-event) because explicit time references are easier to link. TimeQA contains 5.5K time-evolving facts across ~1.5K entities (~3.7 facts/entity); Easy questions involve direct temporal extraction (lower d), Hard questions require cross-fact inference (higher effective N). Stage 1 measures actual N and d to validate these estimates. The key falsifiable prediction: verification uplift (EM gain from adding consistency checking) should correlate positively with predicted P_detect across benchmarks.

(d) **Formula Assumptions and Limitations**: P_detect relies on four simplifying assumptions that we explicitly state: (i) *Triangle independence* — overlapping triangles sharing edges create correlated detection events. In sparse graphs with few triangles, independence is approximately satisfied and P_detect serves as a reasonable estimate; in dense graphs with many overlapping triangles, the formula is an optimistic upper bound, but detection is already near-certain so the bound remains informative. (ii) *Erdős-Rényi random graph structure* — d² assumes each edge exists independently with probability d. Real temporal graphs exhibit locality bias (events close in narrative tend to have more extracted relations), which may create dense local subgraphs that boost local detection beyond what global d predicts. This means P_detect may UNDERESTIMATE detection for structured temporal narratives with tight event clusters. (iii) *Uniform relation-type distribution* — τ_uniform=0.88 assumes equal probability over all 13 relation types, but real temporal data is heavily skewed toward before/after. We mitigate this by computing a weighted τ_w = Σ_{r1,r2} P(R=r1)·P(R=r2)·(13-|C(r1,r2)|)/12 using observed relation frequencies from each benchmark. Notably, before∘before and after∘after are singletons (τ=1.0), but before∘after yields the full 13-relation set (τ=0), so heavy before/after skew creates bimodal detection: same-direction triangles detect perfectly while opposite-direction triangles detect nothing. (iv) *Binary detection* — we treat compositions as either detecting (wrong relation outside set) or not. In practice, size-3 and size-5 result sets provide graduated constraint, narrowing the space of consistent relations and enabling probabilistic inference even when they don't definitively reject the wrong relation. This binary model is conservative: actual detection capability is weakly higher. The synthetic corruption experiment (Stage 2f) explicitly validates P_detect against empirical detection rates across controlled density conditions, quantifying the gap introduced by these assumptions.

(e) **Concrete practitioner decision boundary with worked example**: A practitioner building a temporal QA system can estimate N and d for their data, then compute P_detect. We identify the threshold where verification's expected benefit (P_detect × accuracy_gain_per_detected_error) exceeds its cost (formalization errors × accuracy_loss_per_false_correction + compute overhead). Our estimate: verification becomes cost-effective when P_detect > 0.3, corresponding to d > ~0.31 for N=6 with τ=0.88. Importantly, practitioners can implement this check as O(n³) path-consistency — no SMT solver is needed, as path-consistency is complete for basic Allen relations.

**Worked example**: A developer building a temporal QA system measures N≈5 events per question context and d≈0.25 extractable density (typical of TimeQA Easy). They compute P_detect ≈ 1-(1-0.0625·0.88)^3 ≈ 0.16. Since P_detect=0.16 is well below the 0.3 cost-effectiveness threshold, they should invest compute budget in improved extraction (e.g., grammar-constrained decoding, redundant extraction) rather than adding verification overhead. Conversely, a developer working with TGQA-style data (N≈8, d≈0.35) computes P_detect≈0.50, exceeding the threshold — here, adding O(n³) path-consistency checking is justified.

(f) **Synthetic corruption experiment**: Inject controlled errors (relation misclassification, entity swaps, omissions) into gold temporal graphs at 10/20/30/40% corruption rates across varying graph densities. Measure detection rates by path-consistency, validating the theoretical P_detect formula against empirical results and quantifying the gap from the simplifying assumptions.

(g) **Detection coverage by error type**: Omission errors (expected: ~0% detection — removing a constraint cannot create inconsistency); relation misclassification (expected: density-dependent, governed by composition tightness of the triangle); hallucinated relations (expected: moderate detection — adding a wrong relation to an existing consistent graph may create new triangles). This decomposition is absent from both Eirew et al. and Kougia et al.

(h) **Comparison across verification paradigms**: Compare consistency-based detection coverage against (i) LLM-based abductive reflection (NeSTR-style), (ii) simple heuristic checks (range validation, symmetry checking), and (iii) redundant cross-step extraction (re-extracting previously established relations from new CoT contexts to create multiple constraint paths — tested as an ablation to measure whether redundancy boosts P_detect by increasing effective density). The key question: does consistency checking's formal guarantees provide meaningfully higher detection than simpler alternatives?

(i) **Generalizability to other constraint domains**: The composition tightness framework applies to ANY qualitative constraint calculus with a composition table. We precisely characterize two additional domains:

(i) **RCC-8 spatial reasoning**: We compute the full 8×8=64 entry composition table (from Randell, Cui & Cohn, 1992; verified against Renz & Nebel). The exact result-set size distribution is: 27 singletons (42.2%), 4 size-2 entries (6.3%), 8 size-3 (12.5%), 3 size-4 (4.7%), 16 size-5 (25.0%), 3 size-6 (4.7%), and 3 universal/size-8 entries (4.7%). The per-triangle detection probability uses (8-|S|)/7, yielding τ_uniform(RCC-8) = [27×1.0 + 4×(6/7) + 8×(5/7) + 3×(4/7) + 16×(3/7) + 3×(2/7) + 3×0]/64 = 45.6/64 ≈ 0.71 — substantially lower than Allen's τ=0.88. This predicts lower detection coverage for spatial verification at equivalent graph densities. Notably, 16 of 64 entries (25%) are size-5 (containing 5 of 8 relations), providing only (3/7)≈0.43 detection probability per triangle — these large-but-not-universal result sets dominate in RCC-8 far more than in Allen's algebra, driving the tightness gap.

(ii) **Event coreference transitivity**: A degenerate case with just 2 basic relations (coreferent/non-coreferent), where composition is deterministic (τ=1.0) — every triangle with inconsistent labels is detected. This explains why transitivity enforcement consistently helps coreference resolution (Finkel & Manning, 2008; up to 3.6% B³ improvement / 16.5% cluster F-score).

These cross-domain comparisons demonstrate the framework's generality and provide actionable predictions for researchers in spatial reasoning and coreference.

**Stage 3 (Pipeline Implementation — Research Vehicle):** Per-step temporal assertion extraction → incremental path-consistency checking (O(n³), complete for basic Allen relations per Nebel & Bürckert) with confidence-weighted soft/hard constraints → verify-and-correct loop with MCS (minimal correction set) feedback (max 5 iterations). For MCS computation under weighted preferences, we optionally compare path-consistency-based greedy MCS against ILP-based optimal MCS. This pipeline serves as the vehicle for measuring detection coverage and formalization feasibility in context, not as a claimed SOTA system. We explicitly measure both per-step and full-context extraction and report the comparison without claiming either is superior a priori.

**Stage 4 (Standard Benchmark Evaluation — Contextualized):** Evaluate on TGQA, TempReason (L2/L3), TimeQA (Easy/Hard), TCP — NOT to claim SOTA but to measure verification uplift (or deficit) against no-verification baselines using the same backbone. We compare against NeSTR's abductive reflection (85.2 EM, GPT-4o-mini; 84.5 EM / 88.8 F1, Qwen3-14B) to contextualize. If verification hurts on sparse QA graphs (as our formula predicts for TimeQA Easy with P_detect≈0.16), this validates the formal analysis. The KEY test: does the rank ordering of verification uplift across benchmarks match the rank ordering of predicted P_detect? If TGQA shows the highest uplift and TimeQA Easy the lowest, the framework is validated.

**Key Ablations:** (1) Path-consistency verification vs. NeSTR-style abductive reflection vs. no verification vs. simple heuristic checks — isolating consistency checking's marginal value; (2) Unconstrained vs. structured-output vs. grammar-constrained formalization — measuring formalization technique impact; (3) Single-path vs. redundant cross-step extraction — measuring whether redundancy boosts effective density and detection coverage (this tests whether redundancy is a viable technique for overcoming sparse-graph limitations); (4) Sparse (standard QA) vs. dense (document-level) constraint graphs — validating the detection probability formula across the density spectrum; (5) Uniform τ vs. weighted τ_w — measuring the impact of relation distribution skew on detection coverage predictions.

**Negative Result Contingency (Explicit):** If detection coverage is low (<30% on standard QA's sparse graphs) and verification provides no significant uplift over no-verification baselines, the paper reframes as a definitive cautionary finding — analogous to 'Right for the Wrong Reasons' (McCoy et al., ACL 2019). Specifically: (a) the first FORMAL evidence (not just empirical observation) that consistency-based verification (regardless of solver) is not justified for temporal QA with sparse constraint graphs; (b) a quantitative density threshold formula practitioners can use; (c) a recommendation to invest in improved extraction rather than verification overhead for standard QA tasks, with verification reserved for document-level tasks with dense temporal annotations.

**Critical Differentiation from Eirew et al. (EMNLP 2025):** Our work differs on five dimensions: (1) TASK: we study temporal QA verification (checking extracted facts during CoT reasoning), not temporal relation extraction (classifying all event pairs in documents) — different error distributions and graph structures; (2) ANALYSIS TYPE: we provide a formal framework (composition tightness, detection probability formula P_detect ≈ 1-(1-d²·τ)^(N-2)) that EXPLAINS why density matters, vs. their empirical observation; (3) ERROR TYPE DECOMPOSITION: we decompose detection by omission/misclassification/hallucination — they don't; (4) FORMALIZATION FEASIBILITY: we address whether LLMs can formalize temporal NL into Allen's vocabulary (Stage 0) — they assume extraction works; (5) DECISION BOUNDARY: we provide a quantitative threshold formula for practitioners — they don't. Additionally, our framework is SOLVER-AGNOSTIC, subsuming their ILP-specific approach.

**Risk Discussion — arXiv:2605.04243:** This preprint (single author, high school affiliation, no code released, unreviewed) is cited only for two independently verifiable observations: (1) verification fails on omission errors (a logical consequence of any consistency-based approach); (2) extraction quality bounds system performance (consistent with TMLR 2025). Our analysis stands entirely independently.

  "core_problem": "Multiple verification paradigms — consistency-based (path-consistency, ILP, SMT), probabilistic (credal intervals + EDL), and neural (abductive reflection) — have been proposed for catching temporal extraction errors in neuro-symbolic QA, but a fundamental empirical question remains unanswered: what fraction of extraction errors actually produce detectable inconsistencies, and under what conditions? Crucially, Nebel & Bürckert (JACM 1995) prove that for basic Allen relations (a subset of ORD-Horn), path-consistency is COMPLETE for detecting all inconsistencies in O(n³) time. We also catalog failure modes specific to temporal formalization: implicit relations, vague temporal references ('around that time'), relative expressions ('shortly after'), and missing event instantiation. If formalization success is <60% even with constrained decoding, this is itself a key finding that quantifies the formalization gap for Allen's relations specifically.

**Stage 1 (Constraint Graph Density Characterization):** We measure the density of temporal constraint graphs extractable from standard QA benchmarks (TGQA, TempReason L2/L3, TimeQA Easy/Hard), reporting: (a) average number of temporal entities per question; (b) average extractable Allen relations; (c) graph density ratio (edges / max possible edges); (d) constraint redundancy via transitivity. This analysis applies to ANY consistency-based approach — path-consistency, ILP, or SMT — since Nebel & Bürckert (JACM 1995) prove that path-consistency alone is complete for basic Allen relations.

(a) **Composition tightness analysis**: Allen's 169 basic-relation compositions yield result sets of exactly 1, 3, 5, 9, or 13 relations (a known mathematical property). We compute these PRECISELY from the published composition table (Alspaugh's Table 4b): 97 entries (57.4%) are singletons — broken down by relation as p(22), P(22), d(9), D(9), m(6), M(6), o(5), O(5), s(3), S(3), f(3), F(3), e(1) — with 42 entries (24.9%) yielding size-3 sets, 24 (14.2%) yielding size-5, 3 (1.8%) yielding size-9 (the 'concur' set), and 3 (1.8%) yielding the full 13-relation set. Singletons guarantee detection of any wrong relation; the full set provides zero detection capability. The per-triangle detection probability for a uniformly random misclassification is (13-|S|)/12, giving: size-1 → 1.0, size-3 → 0.833, size-5 → 0.667, size-9 → 0.333, size-13 → 0. The unweighted average composition tightness is τ_uniform = [97×1.0 + 42×0.833 + 24×0.667 + 3×0.333 + 3×0]/169 = 149/169 ≈ 0.88. For empirical analysis, we compute a weighted τ_w using the observed relation frequency distribution from each benchmark, since real data is skewed toward before/after.

(b) **Detection probability formula**: For N events, graph density d, and average composition tightness τ, the probability of detecting a wrong relation R(A,C) via at least one triangle A-B-C is: P_detect ≈ 1 - (1 - d²·τ)^(N-2). Pattern: analogous to how 'Right for the Wrong Reasons' (McCoy et al., ACL 2019) provided diagnostic insight into NLI beyond mere accuracy numbers.",
  "approach": "We propose a diagnostic study — TemporalCoT-Verify — that answers 'When does consistency checking help catch temporal extraction errors in LLM chain-of-thought reasoning?' through four contributions: a formalization feasibility pilot, constraint graph density characterization, a formal detection coverage framework based on Allen's composition table tightness, and systematic empirical validation. The pipeline is a research vehicle for this analysis, not a SOTA-seeking system. Our detection coverage framework is SOLVER-AGNOSTIC: Nebel & Bürckert (JACM 1995) prove that for basic Allen relations (subset of ORD-Horn), path-consistency is COMPLETE for detecting all inconsistencies in O(n³). This means the detection coverage limits we characterize are FUNDAMENTAL to the constraint language — they hold identically for path-consistency, ILP (Eirew et al.), or SMT solvers. Practitioners can use the simplest adequate solver.

**Stage 0 (Formalization Feasibility Pilot — Prerequisite Validation):** We conduct a pilot measuring whether LLMs can reliably formalize temporal statements from QA text into Allen's 13-relation vocabulary. Amonkar et al. (arXiv 2505.13252) show formalization challenges on general CSPs, but Allen's fixed 13-way vocabulary is substantially more constrained. ChronoSense (ACL 2025, v2) shows GPT-4o achieves 0.877 accuracy classifying Allen relations WITH explicit intervals given (average of 13 Allen-specific zero-shot accuracies from Table 2, ranging from 0.69 for Equals to 0.956 for After); we estimate extraction from natural language text (without explicit intervals) will yield 0.55-0.70 accuracy with structured-output constraints and 0.40-0.60 unconstrained, based on: (a) the gap between structured classification and open-ended extraction observed across NLU tasks; (b) the additional difficulty of identifying implicit temporal boundaries; (c) VeriCoT's 15-45% pass rate on the harder task of general CoT→FOL formalization (Allen classification is substantially easier). This analysis applies to ANY consistency-based approach — path-consistency, ILP, or SMT — since Nebel & Bürckert (JACM 1995) prove that path-consistency alone is complete for basic Allen relations.

(a) **Composition tightness analysis**: Allen's 169 basic-relation compositions yield result sets of exactly 1, 3, 5, 9, or 13 relations (a known mathematical property). We compute these PRECISELY from the published composition table (Alspaugh's Table 4b): 97 entries (57.4%) are singletons — broken down by relation as p(22), P(22), d(9), D(9), m(6), M(6), o(5), O(5), s(3), S(3), f(3), F(3), e(1) — with 42 entries (24.9%) yielding size-3 sets, 24 (14.2%) yielding size-5, 3 (1.8%) yielding size-9 (the 'concur' set), and 3 (1.8%) yielding the full 13-relation set. Singletons guarantee detection of any wrong relation; the full set provides zero detection capability. The per-triangle detection probability for a uniformly random misclassification is (13-|S|)/12, giving: size-1 → 1.0, size-3 → 0.833, size-5 → 0.667, size-9 → 0.333, size-13 → 0. The unweighted average composition tightness is τ_uniform = [97×1.0 + 42×0.833 + 24×0.667 + 3×0.333 + 3×0]/169 = 149/169 ≈ 0.88. For empirical analysis, we compute a weighted τ_w using the observed relation frequency distribution from each benchmark, since real data is skewed toward before/after.

(b) **Detection probability formula**: For N events, graph density d, and average composition tightness τ, the probability of detecting a wrong relation R(A,C) via at least one triangle A-B-C is: P_detect ≈ 1 - (1 - d²·τ)^(N-2). This formula explains the Eirew et al. results quantitatively: for sparse MATRES-like graphs (N≈22, d≈0.21 given 79% missing), P_detect ≈ 0.55; for dense OmniTemp-like graphs (N≈16, d≈1.0), P_detect approaches 1.0.

(c) **Prospective predictions for temporal QA benchmarks**: We pre-commit to specific P_detect predictions for each benchmark BEFORE running experiments, based on preliminary N and d estimates from dataset documentation and sampling:

| Benchmark       | Est. N | Est. d | Predicted P_detect | Prediction |
|-----------------|--------|--------|--------------------|------------|
| TGQA            | 8      | 0.35   | 0.50               | Moderate detection; verification may provide modest uplift |
| TempReason L2   | 5      | 0.33   | 0.26               | Near threshold; marginal benefit expected |
| TempReason L3   | 5      | 0.30   | 0.22               | Below threshold; verification likely not cost-effective |
| TimeQA Easy     | 5      | 0.25   | 0.16               | Well below threshold; verification not justified |
| TimeQA Hard     | 6      | 0.30   | 0.28               | Near threshold; may show small uplift |

Estimation basis: TGQA stories are generated from YAGO11k subgraphs with 5-28 temporal events per story (TG-LLM, ACL 2024) and ~9 temporal facts per sample; N≈8 reflects the median entity count, d≈0.35 reflects extractable pairwise relations relative to maximum edges. TempReason subjects have ~5.3 temporal facts (Tan et al., 2023); L2 (time-event) has slightly higher extractable density than L3 (event-event) because explicit time references are easier to link. TimeQA contains 5.5K time-evolving facts across ~1.5K entities (~3.7 facts/entity); Easy questions involve direct temporal extraction (lower d), Hard questions require cross-fact inference (higher effective N). Stage 1 measures actual N and d to validate these estimates. The key falsifiable prediction: verification uplift (EM gain from adding consistency checking) should correlate positively with predicted P_detect across benchmarks.

(d) **Formula Assumptions and Limitations**: P_detect relies on four simplifying assumptions that we explicitly state: (i) *Triangle independence* — overlapping triangles sharing edges create correlated detection events. In sparse graphs with few triangles, independence is approximately satisfied and P_detect serves as a reasonable estimate; in dense graphs with many overlapping triangles, the formula is an optimistic upper bound, but detection is already near-certain so the bound remains informative. (ii) *Erdős-Rényi random graph structure* — d² assumes each edge exists independently with probability d. Real temporal graphs exhibit locality bias (events close in narrative tend to have more extracted relations), which may create dense local subgraphs that boost local detection beyond what global d predicts. This means P_detect may UNDERESTIMATE detection for structured temporal narratives with tight event clusters. (iii) *Uniform relation-type distribution* — τ_uniform=0.88 assumes equal probability over all 13 relation types, but real temporal data is heavily skewed toward before/after. We mitigate this by computing a weighted τ_w = Σ_{r1,r2} P(R=r1)·P(R=r2)·(13-|C(r1,r2)|)/12 using observed relation frequencies from each benchmark. Notably, before∘before and after∘after are singletons (τ=1.0), but before∘after yields the full 13-relation set (τ=0), so heavy before/after skew creates bimodal detection: same-direction triangles detect perfectly while opposite-direction triangles detect nothing. (iv) *Binary detection* — we treat compositions as either detecting (wrong relation outside set) or not. In practice, size-3 and size-5 result sets provide graduated constraint, narrowing the space of consistent relations and enabling probabilistic inference even when they don't definitively reject the wrong relation. This binary model is conservative: actual detection capability is weakly higher. The synthetic corruption experiment (Stage 2f) explicitly validates P_detect against empirical detection rates across controlled density conditions, quantifying the gap introduced by these assumptions.

(e) **Concrete practitioner decision boundary with worked example**: A practitioner building a temporal QA system can estimate N and d for their data, then compute P_detect. We identify the threshold where verification's expected benefit (P_detect × accuracy_gain_per_detected_error) exceeds its cost (formalization errors × accuracy_loss_per_false_correction + compute overhead). Our estimate: verification becomes cost-effective when P_detect > 0.3, corresponding to d > ~0.31 for N=6 with τ=0.88. Importantly, practitioners can implement this check as O(n³) path-consistency — no SMT solver is needed, as path-consistency is complete for basic Allen relations.

**Worked example**: A developer building a temporal QA system measures N≈5 events per question context and d≈0.25 extractable density (typical of TimeQA Easy). They compute P_detect ≈ 1-(1-0.0625·0.88)^3 ≈ 0.16. Since P_detect=0.16 is well below the 0.3 cost-effectiveness threshold, they should invest compute budget in improved extraction (e.g., grammar-constrained decoding, redundant extraction) rather than adding verification overhead. Conversely, a developer working with TGQA-style data (N≈8, d≈0.35) computes P_detect≈0.50, exceeding the threshold — here, adding O(n³) path-consistency checking is justified.

(f) **Synthetic corruption experiment**: Inject controlled errors (relation misclassification, entity swaps, omissions) into gold temporal graphs at 10/20/30/40% corruption rates across varying graph densities. Measure detection rates by path-consistency, validating the theoretical P_detect formula against empirical results and quantifying the gap from the simplifying assumptions.

(g) **Detection coverage by error type**: Omission errors (expected: ~0% detection — removing a constraint cannot create inconsistency); relation misclassification (expected: density-dependent, governed by composition tightness of the triangle); hallucinated relations (expected: moderate detection — adding a wrong relation to an existing consistent graph may create new triangles). This decomposition is absent from both Eirew et al. and Kougia et al.

(h) **Comparison across verification paradigms**: Compare consistency-based detection coverage against (i) LLM-based abductive reflection (NeSTR-style), (ii) simple heuristic checks (range validation, symmetry checking), and (iii) redundant cross-step extraction (re-extracting previously established relations from new CoT contexts to create multiple constraint paths — tested as an ablation to measure whether redundancy boosts P_detect by increasing effective density). The key question: does consistency checking's formal guarantees provide meaningfully higher detection than simpler alternatives?

(i) **Generalizability to other constraint domains**: The composition tightness framework applies to ANY qualitative constraint calculus with a composition table. We precisely characterize two additional domains:

(i) **RCC-8 spatial reasoning**: We compute the full 8×8=64 entry composition table (from Randell, Cui & Cohn, 1992; verified against Renz & Nebel). The exact result-set size distribution is: 27 singletons (42.2%), 4 size-2 entries (6.3%), 8 size-3 (12.5%), 3 size-4 (4.7%), 16 size-5 (25.0%), 3 size-6 (4.7%), and 3 universal/size-8 entries (4.7%). The per-triangle detection probability uses (8-|S|)/7, yielding τ_uniform(RCC-8) = [27×1.0 + 4×(6/7) + 8×(5/7) + 3×(4/7) + 16×(3/7) + 3×(2/7) + 3×0]/64 = 45.6/64 ≈ 0.71 — substantially lower than Allen's τ=0.88. This predicts lower detection coverage for spatial verification at equivalent graph densities. Notably, 16 of 64 entries (25%) are size-5 (containing 5 of 8 relations), providing only (3/7)≈0.43 detection probability per triangle — these large-but-not-universal result sets dominate in RCC-8 far more than in Allen's algebra, driving the tightness gap.

(ii) **Event coreference transitivity**: A degenerate case with just 2 basic relations (coreferent/non-coreferent), where composition is deterministic (τ=1.0) — every triangle with inconsistent labels is detected. This explains why transitivity enforcement consistently helps coreference resolution (Finkel & Manning, 2008; up to 3.6% B³ improvement / 16.5% cluster F-score).

These cross-domain comparisons demonstrate the framework's generality and provide actionable predictions for researchers in spatial reasoning and coreference.

**Stage 3 (Pipeline Implementation — Research Vehicle):** Per-step temporal assertion extraction → incremental path-consistency checking (O(n³), complete for basic Allen relations per Nebel & Bürckert) with confidence-weighted soft/hard constraints → verify-and-correct loop with MCS (minimal correction set) feedback (max 5 iterations). For MCS computation under weighted preferences, we optionally compare path-consistency-based greedy MCS against ILP-based optimal MCS. This pipeline serves as the vehicle for measuring detection coverage and formalization feasibility in context, not as a claimed SOTA system. We explicitly measure both per-step and full-context extraction and report the comparison without claiming either is superior a priori.

**Stage 4 (Standard Benchmark Evaluation — Contextualized):** Evaluate on TGQA, TempReason (L2/L3), TimeQA (Easy/Hard), TCP — NOT to claim SOTA but to measure verification uplift (or deficit) against no-verification baselines using the same backbone. We compare against NeSTR's abductive reflection (85.2 EM, GPT-4o-mini; 84.5 EM / 88.8 F1, Qwen3-14B) to contextualize. If verification hurts on sparse QA graphs (as our formula predicts for TimeQA Easy with P_detect≈0.16), this validates the formal analysis. The KEY test: does the rank ordering of verification uplift across benchmarks match the rank ordering of predicted P_detect? If TGQA shows the highest uplift and TimeQA Easy the lowest, the framework is validated.

**Key Ablations:** (1) Path-consistency verification vs. NeSTR-style abductive reflection vs. no verification vs. simple heuristic checks — isolating consistency checking's marginal value; (2) Unconstrained vs. structured-output vs. grammar-constrained formalization — measuring formalization technique impact; (3) Single-path vs. redundant cross-step extraction — measuring whether redundancy boosts effective density and detection coverage (this tests whether redundancy is a viable technique for overcoming sparse-graph limitations); (4) Sparse (standard QA) vs. dense (document-level) constraint graphs — validating the detection probability formula across the density spectrum; (5) Uniform τ vs. weighted τ_w — measuring the impact of relation distribution skew on detection coverage predictions.

**Negative Result Contingency (Explicit):** If detection coverage is low (<30% on standard QA's sparse graphs) and verification provides no significant uplift over no-verification baselines, the paper reframes as a definitive cautionary finding — analogous to 'Right for the Wrong Reasons' (McCoy et al., ACL 2019). Specifically: (a) the first FORMAL evidence (not just empirical observation) that consistency-based verification (regardless of solver) is not justified for temporal QA with sparse constraint graphs; (b) a quantitative density threshold formula practitioners can use; (c) a recommendation to invest in improved extraction rather than verification overhead for standard QA tasks, with verification reserved for document-level tasks with dense temporal annotations.

**Critical Differentiation from Eirew et al. (EMNLP 2025):** Our work differs on five dimensions: (1) TASK: we study temporal QA verification (checking extracted facts during CoT reasoning), not temporal relation extraction (classifying all event pairs in documents) — different error distributions and graph structures; (2) ANALYSIS TYPE: we provide a formal framework (composition tightness, detection probability formula P_detect ≈ 1-(1-d²·τ)^(N-2)) that EXPLAINS why density matters, vs. their empirical observation; (3) ERROR TYPE DECOMPOSITION: we decompose detection by omission/misclassification/hallucination — they don't; (4) FORMALIZATION FEASIBILITY: we address whether LLMs can formalize temporal NL into Allen's vocabulary (Stage 0) — they assume extraction works; (5) DECISION BOUNDARY: we provide a quantitative threshold formula for practitioners — they don't. Additionally, our framework is SOLVER-AGNOSTIC, subsuming their ILP-specific approach.

**Risk Discussion — arXiv:2605.04243:** This preprint (single author, high school affiliation, no code released, unreviewed) is cited only for two independently verifiable observations: (1) verification fails on omission errors (a logical consequence of any consistency-based approach); (2) extraction quality bounds system performance (consistent with TMLR 2025). Our analysis stands entirely independently.
